title: Devlens Research Summary: Where Bangladesh's child marriage and fertility gaps are widest
excerpt: A new BBS-UNICEF district atlas from MICS 2025 shows child marriage ranging from 12.8% in Sylhet to 73.3% in Joypurhat, and fertility from 1.5 in Bagerhat to 3.5 in Bhola.

image.alt: Women raking grain to dry in a village in Bangladesh

content:
Where a girl grows up in Bangladesh still shapes how likely she is to be married as a child, how many children she will have and how she will be disciplined at home. A new district atlas from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and UNICEF puts numbers on those gaps for all 64 districts. In Joypurhat, nearly three in four young women were married before 18. In Sylhet district, the figure is about one in eight. This summary sets out what it shows and what it means for programmes.

The source

The Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025: District Atlas was published by BBS on Tuesday, 24 November, according to The Business Standard. It breaks down results from MICS 2025, the seventh round of the survey, which BBS runs with technical and financial support from UNICEF.

According to the survey's preliminary report, published in November 2025, field teams interviewed 62,980 households in 3,149 clusters between mid-February and mid-June 2025. The sample was spread evenly at about 940 households per reporting area so that each of the 64 districts and three city corporations has its own estimates. The fertility rate is calculated from women aged 15 to 49 and covers the three years before the survey.

Where things stand

The national picture, from the preliminary report, is mixed. Child marriage is falling slowly: 47.2% of women aged 20 to 24 were married before 18, down from 51.4% in 2019 and 52.3% in 2012-13. But the share of girls aged 15 to 19 who are currently married rose from 32.9% in 2019 to 38.9%. The adolescent birth rate rose from 83 to 92 births per 1,000 girls aged 15 to 19.

The total fertility rate (TFR), the average number of children a woman is expected to have, rose from 2.3 to 2.4. It had stayed at 2.3 in both 2012-13 and 2019. Over the same period, the share of married women using any contraceptive method fell from 62.7% to 58.2%. The share whose family planning needs were met with modern methods fell from 77.4% to 73.5%.

Finding 1: a two-child gap in fertility between districts

Bhola has the country's highest TFR at 3.5 children per woman, and Bagerhat the lowest at 1.5, as reported by The Business Standard from the atlas. Madaripur (3.3) and Noakhali (3.0) follow Bhola. Lakshmipur, Sunamganj and Barishal are at 2.9, and Brahmanbaria, Sherpur and Gaibandha at 2.8.

At the other end, Jashore, Rajbari and Naogaon are at 1.7, Kushtia and Manikganj at 1.8, and Gazipur, Meherpur and Rajshahi at 1.9.

Finding 2: child marriage is concentrated in the west and north

Joypurhat has the highest child marriage rate, with 73.3% of women aged 20 to 24 married before 18. Chuadanga (67.9%), Bhola (65%), Sirajganj (63.1%), Kushtia (62.9%), Jashore (62.3%), Tangail (61.1%) and Magura (61.1%) follow. Bogura (55.2%) and Pabna (52.6%) are also above half.

Sylhet district has the lowest rate, at 12.8%. Sunamganj and Moulvibazar are at 24.4% and Habiganj at 27.4%. This matches the preliminary report, which found the highest rates in Rajshahi (67%) and Khulna (65%) divisions and the lowest in Sylhet (29%), using a wider measure of all women aged 18 to 49.

The two maps do not line up neatly. Jashore and Kushtia are among the districts with the lowest fertility, yet more than six in ten young women there married as children. Sunamganj has high fertility but relatively low child marriage.

Finding 3: violent discipline is almost universal in some districts

Nationally, 85.7% of children aged 1 to 14 experienced physical punishment or psychological aggression from adults at home in the month before the survey. That is down from 88.8% in 2019 but above the 82.3% of 2012-13. The preliminary report found that only 9% of children experienced only non-violent discipline, and about a third of mothers and caregivers (32%) believe physical punishment is necessary.

By district, the rate reaches 98.8% in Bandarban, 95.4% in Dinajpur, 94.2% in Rajshahi, 93.8% in Thakurgaon and 93.6% in Khagrachhari. Sylhet is again lowest, at 63.5%, followed by Chandpur (71.2%), Barguna (73.6%) and Naogaon (75.1%).

What it means for the development sector

Targeting. The atlas gives NGOs, donors and government departments a common, official basis for choosing where to work. Child marriage programmes have a clear case for concentrating on Joypurhat, Chuadanga, Sirajganj, Kushtia, Jashore and Bhola. Family planning work has a case for Bhola, Madaripur, Noakhali and the Sunamganj haor.

Family planning services. Rising fertility and falling contraceptive use come at a time of strain for the family planning system. Prothom Alo reported in July that 27% of posts in the Directorate General of Family Planning were vacant and that field-level contraceptive supplies had run short. The government is now folding family planning field staff into a new primary healthcare department. Dhaka University population scientist Mohammad Mainul Islam told The Business Standard that the Family Planning Strategy 2025-2030 needs to be fully implemented, with more field staff, steady supplies and targets for high-fertility districts.

Child marriage law. The atlas comes as UNFPA and UNICEF push to reform the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, including repealing Section 19, which allows marriage below the legal age in "special circumstances". District figures give campaigners and local child marriage prevention committees evidence to hold officials to account.

Parenting and child protection. Near-universal violent discipline in Bandarban, Khagrachhari and parts of the north points to a need for positive parenting and community-based child protection work, especially in the Chittagong Hill Tracts.

Limits of the evidence

Devlens has not seen the district atlas itself. The BBS website was unreachable on Wednesday morning, and the district figures in this summary come from The Business Standard's report. The national figures were checked against the MICS 2025 preliminary report published by UNICEF Bangladesh.

There is one discrepancy readers should note. The Business Standard reports divisional fertility rates from the atlas of 2.0 for Khulna and 2.6 for Barishal, with Mymensingh at 2.4. The preliminary report gave 2.3 for Khulna, 2.4 for Barishal and 2.8 for Mymensingh. The atlas may use revised data or a different calculation, or the press figures may be wrong. Organisations should check the atlas before using divisional numbers.

District estimates rest on about 940 households each, so they carry wider margins of error than national figures, and small differences between districts may not be meaningful. The data were collected in early 2025.

The bottom line

Bangladesh's national averages hide very different realities. A girl in Joypurhat is almost six times as likely to be married as a child as one in Sylhet district, and a woman in Bhola is expected to have more than twice as many children as one in Bagerhat. With fertility rising for the first time in decades and contraceptive use falling, the atlas is a tool for putting scarce family planning and child protection resources where they are needed most.
